name: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides

clinicalPearls: Acromegaly drives an osteoarthritis-like picture from growth hormone/IGF-I overstimulation of cartilage and bone; prominent wrist involvement (unusual for primary OA), early radiographic joint-space WIDENING from cartilage hypertrophy, carpal tunnel syndrome in roughly half, and Raynaud phenomenon in about a third.

In hemochromatosis, arthropathy may be the FIRST clinical clue: degenerative-type involvement that characteristically starts at the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints (joints generally spared by routine OA), often with hooklike MCP osteophytes and frequent calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

An early hemochromatosis diagnosis is suggested by a high serum transferrin saturation, which is more sensitive than ferritin elevation; dominant 2nd/3rd MCP findings warrant ferritin and iron/total iron-binding capacity testing.

Hemophilic recurrent spontaneous hemarthrosis (factor VIII or IX deficiency) typically begins after age 1 when the child walks/runs and targets knees, ankles, elbows, shoulders, and hips, progressing to chronic fibrotic deforming arthropathy.
Hemarthrosis is characteristic of hemophilia but NOT of von Willebrand disease, factor V deficiency, oral anticoagulation, or thrombocytopenia.

Low-grade temperature can accompany acute hemarthrosis, but fever above 38.3 C (101 F) should raise concern for joint infection and prompt aspiration; clotting factor should be corrected before arthrocentesis.

Sickle cell dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children under 5 produces diffuse swelling/tenderness of hands and feet from marrow and cortical bone infarction and is rarely seen after age 5; it generally resolves without residual damage.

Distinguishing osteomyelitis from bone infarction in sickle cell disease is clinically difficult; Salmonella is a notably associated cause of osteomyelitis, whereas S. aureus and Streptococcus are the more common organisms in sickle cell septic arthritis.

Up to ~40% of sickle cell patients are hyperuricemic (urate overproduction plus interstitial renal disease) and can develop acute, sometimes polyarticular, gouty arthritis; arthrocentesis distinguishes gout from infection or synovial infarction.

Achilles tendinitis and migratory large-joint arthritis can be the first clinical sign of familial hypercholesterolemia, preceding the appearance of tendinous xanthomas; synovial fluid is noninflammatory and crystal-negative.

Neuropathic (Charcot) joint disease arises from loss of pain sensation and/or proprioception with impaired protective reflexes; diabetes mellitus is the most frequent cause, classically affecting the tarsal and tarsometatarsal joints.

Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy combines digital clubbing with periosteal new-bone formation; secondary HOA points to intrathoracic malignancy, suppurative/hypoxemic lung disease, congenital heart disease, or hepatopulmonary disease and may precede the underlying illness.
harrison.pathophysiology: These arthritides share the theme of an underlying systemic disorder injuring joints rather than a primary autoimmune synovitis. In acromegaly, excess growth hormone and IGF-I stimulate cartilage, periarticular connective tissue, and bone, producing hypertrophic then degenerating cartilage that is prone to fissuring, with ligamentous laxity worsening joint discomfort. In hemochromatosis, parenchymal iron deposition damages cartilage: iron catalyzes superoxide-dependent lipid peroxidation, interferes with collagen formation, increases lysosomal enzyme release from synovium, and inhibits synovial pyrophosphatase, favoring chondrocalcinosis. Hemophilic arthropathy results from repeated intraarticular bleeding; blood persists because intrinsic clotting factors and tissue thromboplastin are absent in the synovium, and recurrent hemarthrosis leads to chronic noninflammatory fibrotic joints. Sickle cell musculoskeletal disease stems from vasoocclusion and marrow/cortical bone infarction, splenic dysfunction predisposing to osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, and avascular necrosis (notably femoral head); marrow hyperplasia widens medullary cavities and thins cortices. In neuropathic joints, loss of deep pain/proprioception plus dysregulated autonomic blood flow leads to bone resorption, repeated microtrauma, ligament tears, and fractures with progressive disorganization. HOA pathogenesis centers on circulating cells/platelet particles and growth factors (PDGF, VEGF) bypassing pulmonary clearance and stimulating peripheral connective tissue and periosteal proliferation, with endothelial activation reflected by elevated von Willebrand factor antigen.
additionalDifferentials: Primary osteoarthritis (vs acromegalic and hemochromatotic arthropathy, distinguished by atypical joint distribution such as wrist or 2nd/3rd MCP involvement)
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease / pseudogout (frequent in acromegaly and hemochromatosis)
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (spine changes in acromegaly can mimic it)
Osteomyelitis (especially diabetic neuropathic foot and sickle cell disease)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (transfused thalassemia patients may have circulating ANA without SLE)
infectionMimics: Septic arthritis (difficult to distinguish from acute hemarthrosis in hemophilia and from sickle cell joint effusions)
Osteomyelitis (mimics neuropathic arthritis in the diabetic foot and complicates sickle cell disease)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute gout/pseudogout flare (hyperlipidemia-associated migratory arthritis can resemble gout)
Advanced osteoarthritis (overlaps radiographically with neuropathic arthritis)
Sterile synovial infarction in sickle cell crisis (can give a high-neutrophil effusion mimicking infection)
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin saturation (sensitive early marker) plus ferritin and iron/total iron-binding capacity for suspected hemochromatosis
Synovial fluid analysis for cell count and crystals (noninflammatory in most of these arthropathies; xanthochromic/bloody with synovial, cartilage, bone fragments in neuropathic joints)
Clotting factor assays and correction prior to arthrocentesis in hemophilia
MRI (sensitive for early avascular necrosis and helpful in osteomyelitis vs neuropathic joint)
Indium-111-labeled WBC nuclear scan (may show uptake in osteomyelitis but not neuropathic joint; technetium bone scan does NOT discriminate the two)
Anti-HMGCR autoantibody testing in patients with elevated muscle enzymes on statin therapy
Joint/tissue cultures when osteomyelitis cannot be excluded radiographically
redFlags: Fever above 38.3 C (101 F) with an acute hemarthrosis in hemophilia, suggesting joint infection
Femoral neuropathy from iliopsoas hematoma in hemophilia (hip held in flexion with preserved rotation)
Closed-compartment hemorrhage (calf or volar forearm) causing muscle necrosis, neuropathy, and flexion contractures
Diabetic foot with callus/ulcer over metatarsal heads progressing to infected ulcer and osteomyelitis
Rapidly disorganizing (Charcot) joint developing over weeks with pain disproportionately mild for the degree of destruction
New digital clubbing or HOA, which may signal occult intrathoracic malignancy
Statin-associated rising muscle enzymes raising concern for necrotizing autoimmune myopathy
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes are determined largely by the underlying disorder. Acromegalic joint pain may persist even after the acromegaly is treated. In hemochromatosis, established arthritis and chondrocalcinosis often progress despite phlebotomy. Hemophilic hemarthrosis usually resolves with joint function returning to baseline over about two weeks, but recurrent bleeding causes chronic fibrotic, flexion-deformed, function-limiting arthropathy. Sickle cell dactylitis resolves without residual damage, but avascular necrosis (about 5% femoral head involvement) and osteomyelitis carry greater morbidity. Neuropathic joints can disorganize rapidly and are largely unaffected by treating the underlying disease; early recognition and offloading of a diabetic Charcot foot can prevent severe disease. In primary HOA, symptoms typically disappear on reaching adulthood.
pitfalls: Attributing acromegalic or hemochromatotic arthropathy to ordinary osteoarthritis and missing the atypical joint distribution (wrist; 2nd/3rd MCP) that should prompt endocrine or iron-overload workup.
Relying on ferritin alone for early hemochromatosis when transferrin saturation is the more sensitive marker.
Mistaking acute hemarthrosis for septic arthritis (or vice versa) in hemophilia; failing to correct clotting factor before aspirating.
Aspirating a hemophilic intramuscular cyst, which can provoke further bleeding (relatively contraindicated unless secondarily infected, and then only after factor repletion).
Using a technetium bone scan to try to separate osteomyelitis from neuropathic arthritis, since uptake is increased in both.
Overlooking that nonselective NSAIDs impair platelet function and should be avoided where feasible in hemophilic bleeding.
Treating isolated clubbing as benign and missing an associated malignancy or lung/cardiac disease.
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal grading scheme; severity is judged by the staging of the underlying arthropathy. Hemophilic arthropathy progresses radiographically from capsular distention, to juxtaarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions and subchondral cysts, to late joint-space narrowing with osteoarthritis-like bony overgrowth. Neuropathic arthritis evolves from early osteoarthritis-like changes (joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, effusions) to marked destructive/hypertrophic disorganization. HOA progresses from periostitis with a radiolucent zone between new periosteal bone and cortex to multilayered cortical thickening.
management: Treat the underlying systemic disorder, normalising growth hormone and IGF-I in acromegaly, using therapeutic venesection in haemochromatosis, and giving clotting factor replacement in haemophilia
Correct the deficient clotting factor before arthrocentesis in haemophilia, and aspirate an acute haemarthrosis, treating as septic arthritis if fever raises that concern
Analgesia and physiotherapy to control joint pain and preserve function
Prophylactic factor replacement to prevent recurrent haemarthrosis and progressive haemophilic arthropathy
Screen for and manage calcium pyrophosphate deposition and chondrocalcinosis complicating haemochromatosis
Joint replacement or other orthopaedic surgery for advanced or deforming arthropathy
Counsel that arthropathy may persist or progress despite treatment of the underlying disorder, warranting ongoing monitoring
Multidisciplinary referral across endocrinology, hepatology, haematology, rheumatology and orthopaedics, with genetic counselling for hereditary haemochromatosis and haemophilia
